key_features.classic_presentation: Acute gastroenteritis presents with crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea (often watery), nausea, and vomiting. Pain is diffuse, not localized. Onset within hours of exposure. Often have known sick contacts or food exposure.
key_features.typical_demographics: All ages. More severe in very young, elderly, and immunocompromised. Viral > bacterial in developed countries.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Infection or inflammation of GI tract (viral, bacterial, or toxin-mediated) leads to increased motility and fluid secretion.

diagnostic_questions.context: Diarrhea is the hallmark of gastroenteritis. Ask about frequency, consistency, and presence of blood.
Crampy, intermittent pain is typical. Constant severe pain suggests alternative diagnosis.
Pain is typically diffuse or periumbilical, not localized to one quadrant.
Vomiting common, often precedes diarrhea. Ask about ability to tolerate fluids.
Low-grade fever typical. High fever suggests bacterial infection or alternative diagnosis.
Known exposure or sick contacts support gastroenteritis diagnosis.
Typical onset 6-48 hours after exposure. Viral: 12-48h, bacterial: 6-24h.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: RLQ pain, anorexia > vomiting/diarrhea, migration pattern
Chronic/recurrent, blood in stool, weight loss
No bowel movements, severe distension, vomiting without diarrhea

red_flags.action: May require IV fluids - go to ER
Possible bacterial infection or IBD - medical evaluation needed
May be appendicitis, diverticulitis, or other serious condition - not simple gastroenteritis

typical_management: Supportive care: oral rehydration, anti-nausea medication if needed. Antibiotics rarely needed (only for specific bacterial infections). Most resolve in 3-7 days.
disposition: Most can be managed at home with oral rehydration. ER if severe dehydration, unable to tolerate fluids, or red flags present.
patient_education: Gastroenteritis (stomach flu) is usually viral and self-limited. Focus on staying hydrated with small frequent sips. Avoid solid foods until vomiting stops. Most people recover in a few days.
